title: Thai Coconut Beef Curry with Potatoes, Peanuts and Tamarind
summary: Beef chuck is slow-braised until fork-tender, then folded through a proper fried massaman paste with potatoes, tamarind and peanuts for a rich, nutty, gently sweet-sour curry.
equipment: large heavy pot or casserole (about 5 l) with a lid

ingredients.item: boneless beef chuck, cut into 5 cm pieces

ingredients.note: check the label: most Thai curry pastes contain shrimp paste (crustaceans); choose a shrimp-free paste if you avoid it

ingredients.item: palm sugar or light brown sugar
waxy potatoes, peeled and cut into 5 cm pieces

steps.title: Brown the beef
steps.text: Pat the beef dry, then heat 1 tbsp oil in the large pot over medium-high heat until shimmering and brown half the beef for 5-6 minutes, turning, until coloured on all sides. Lift it onto a plate and repeat with the remaining oil and beef. Working in batches stops the pot from crowding, so the meat sears and caramelises instead of steaming in its own juices.

steps.title: Braise until tender
steps.text: Return all the beef and its juices to the pot with the cinnamon and star anise, then add enough water to cover, about 2 litres. Bring to a simmer, partly cover and cook at a steady simmer for 1 hour 45 minutes to 2 hours, stirring now and then and topping up water to keep the beef submerged, until a small knife slides in easily. This long, gentle heat slowly melts the tough collagen in chuck into gelatine, which is what makes the meat fall-apart tender.

steps.title: Cool and strain
steps.text: Leave the beef to cool in the braising liquid for 30 minutes, then lift it out and measure 475 ml of the cooking liquid, discarding the spices. Resting in the warm liquid lets the juices settle back through the meat rather than running out as soon as it's cut.

steps.title: Fry the curry paste
steps.text: Put 120 ml of the coconut milk and the 1 tbsp oil in the saucepan over medium-low heat and simmer for 3 minutes, stirring, until slightly thickened. Work in the curry paste hard with the spatula for 2-3 minutes, then keep cooking and scraping while adding another 120 ml coconut milk 2 tbsp at a time over about 10 minutes, until the paste turns a deep reddish brown and oil separates at the edges. This slow frying drives off raw harshness and concentrates the spice oils, and the separating oil is the clearest sign the paste is properly cooked.

steps.title: Season and add potatoes
steps.text: Stir in the sugar, tamarind paste and fish sauce until the sugar melts completely. Add the potatoes and stir to coat them in the fragrant paste. Taste before adding any extra fish sauce, since shop-bought pastes vary a lot in saltiness.

steps.title: Simmer to finish
steps.text: Add the beef, the 475 ml reserved cooking liquid and the remaining 160 ml coconut milk, and bring to a simmer. Cook for about 30 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the sauce is thick with a layer of oil sitting on top; the beef, braised far beyond 63°C, should feel completely fork-tender. Stir in the peanuts and serve with jasmine rice.

tips: Don't crowd the pot when browning the beef — do it in two batches, or the meat will steam rather than brown and you'll lose the deep flavour at the base of the curry.
Check the labels on both the curry paste and fish sauce to make sure they're before buying.
Taste the sauce before adding extra fish sauce for seasoning, as paste saltiness varies between brands.
Keep the paste at a gentle bubble while frying it in step four — rushing the heat can scorch it before the oil has a chance to separate.
This curry freezes well for up to 3 months, though the potatoes may turn a little softer once thawed and reheated.
storage: Cool quickly and refrigerate within 1 hour; use within 3 days and reheat only once until piping hot (74°C). It also freezes well for up to 3 months, though the potatoes may soften slightly on reheating. Cool leftovers in a shallow container and refrigerate within 2 hours (within 1 hour on a day above 32°C).
